info.bio: Faith No More tiene sus orígenes en el año 1981, cuando en California, Mike "The Man" Morris fundaba Faith No Man (acompañado por Mike "Puffy" Bordin, Billy Gould, Mike Morris y Wade Worthington). Un año después, Mike Morris fue expulsado y Wade Worthington fue reemplazado por Roddy Bottum, y el grupo comenzó a llamarse Faith No More. El nombre proviene de una frase de un amigo de la banda: The Man was no more, que literalmente significa "el hombre no estuvo más", haciendo referencia a que habian expulsado a "The Man" (Mike Morris).

scenes.name: Funk metal, arte y autoparodia
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: A principios de los noventa el metal empieza a perder definición en su periferia: el lite metal se acerca al pop con secciones de cuerda (Damn Yankees), otros grupos meten el funk heredado de las mezclas de punk y funk (Living Colour, Faith No More) cortando el poder del metal con ironía, Jane’s Addiction añade art rock reflexivo y Scatterbrain juega con el género de forma consciente, socavando su autenticidad. Weinstein lo ve como el proceso normal de cambio cultural de un género que conserva su núcleo.

scenes.name: MTV y Headbangers Ball
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: MTV nace en agosto de 1981 y en dos años casi monopoliza el videoclip. El heavy, visual desde que Judas Priest se vistió de cuero, es un candidato natural: entre los primeros grupos emitidos están Quiet Riot, Mötley Crüe, Twisted Sister, Dokken y Scorpions, y la cuota de mercado del metal salta del 8 % en 1983 al 20 % en 1984 («MTV fue responsable del resurgir del heavy», dice Dee Snider). A principios de 1985 la presión fundamentalista lo recorta, pero en 1988 nace el programa nocturno «Headbangers Ball». MTV selecciona del metal lo compatible con un público juvenil general: hace del lite metal un coautor del género (pelo cardado, chico malo mono, chicas en el público) y empuja al thrash, casi ausente, a definirse como antítesis comercial. Los vídeos, rodados por directores de publicidad, cuestan cada vez más (190.000 dólares uno de Poison en 1989) y dejan fuera a las bandas pequeñas, convierten los conciertos en simulacros del vídeo y, al llevar el metal al salón familiar, despiertan a sus enemigos: la lista de los «Filthy Fifteen» del PMRC y el departamento de normas de MTV.

scenes.name: Funk-metal
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Una de las grandes ideas de fusión de los ochenta: integrar los ritmos y voces brutales del funk y el rap con el metal de guitarras. Los Red Hot Chili Peppers descubren lo que tenían en común George Clinton y Jello Biafra; Fishbone y su fusión satírica de funk, ska y soul; Faith No More, híbrido inventivo de punk, funk, progresivo, hip hop y metal (Introduce Yourself, Angel Dust); Victim's Family.

podcast.title: Formation and Early Following (1982-1985)
podcast.body: Faith No More formed in San Francisco in 1982 and developed a substantial cult following in the Bay Area by 1985, despite initial difficulties in finding a stable singer. "They were formed in San Francisco in 1982, and by 1985 they had a rather substantial cult following in the Bay area."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Courtney Love Briefly Auditioned (1983); Chuck Mosley Fired After Falling Asleep at Showcase; Mike Patton Took Over
podcast.body: Faith No More evolved from a band called Sharp Young Men, eventually cycling through several singers, including an approximately 20-minute audition by Courtney Love sometime in 1983. Chuck Mosley served as singer from 1983 and recorded their first two albums, but was fired in 1988 after getting into fights with bandmates and roadies, refusing to do anything but acoustic sets, and — most critically — falling asleep on stage during an important showcase performance. His replacement was Mike Patton, who fronted the band for 10 years (1988–1998) and again from 2009 onward. "Epic" remains their biggest song, from Patton's first album with them. "He actually fell asleep on stage during an important showcase event."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Judgment Night Collaboration with Boo-Yaa T.R.I.B.E. (1993)
podcast.body: Faith No More collaborated with hip-hop group Boo-Yaa T.R.I.B.E. for the 1993 *Judgment Night* soundtrack. This pairing was considered radical at the time due to the limited crossover between rock and hip-hop. The project was a major catalyst for the creation of rap rock and nu metal, and helped bridge the divide between rock and hip-hop fans. "The pairings included Pearl Jam and Cypress Hill, Slayer working with Ice Tea, Faith No More and Buella Tribe, Dinosaur Jr., and Del the Funky Homo sapien, 11 collaborations at all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Breakup Announcement (1998)
podcast.body: The band officially broke up on April 19, 1998, after a 15-year run, perhaps due to singer Mike Patton's boredom and desire to explore other projects. Bass player Billy Gould sent out a fax/email stating: "After 15 long and fruitful years, faith no more have decided to put an end to speculation regarding their imminent breakup by breaking up. The decision among the members is mutual and there will be no pointing of fingers, no naming of names other than stating for the record that Puffy started it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Reunion Announcement (2009)
podcast.body: Despite previous denials of any reunion plans, the band announced their return on February 24, 2009, after a separation of 10 years, nine months, and 28 days. The reunion occurred without guitarist Jim Martin. "And on February 24th of 2009, 10 years, nine months, and 28 days after Billy Gould sent out that fax, they know more announced that they were, yes, getting back together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Successful European Tour and New Generation's Interest (2009)
podcast.body: A summer tour of Europe proved "amazingly successful" for the reunited band, coinciding with a new generation of fans discovering their music. "A summer tour of Europe was amazingly successful. And in the interim, a new generation got into this song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: 90s Alternative Success
podcast.body: With Mike Patton as the new singer, Faith No More's 1989 album featuring Patton's lyrics was released in June, received Grammy nominations, and within a year, the band became a prominent fixture on video channels, achieving early success in the alternative 90s. "And within a year, Faith No More was all over the video channels, and we're on their way to becoming one of the biggest early successes of the alternative 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Case for "Bent Band" Inclusion
podcast.body: A case could be made for including Faith No More on a list of "bent" or unconventional artists from the alternative era. "And if you look closely at Faith No More, you can actually make a case for them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Champion Pumpkin Grower
podcast.body: Jim Martin is recognized as one of the most successful growers of champion pumpkins in the United States. "Jim Martin used to be a member of Faith No More is one of the greatest growers of champion pumpkins in all the United States."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chuck Mosley's Erratic Behavior
podcast.body: While Chuck Mosley was the frontman for the band's first two albums, his behavior became increasingly problematic. He got into fights with other band members, sometimes even on stage. He had his own roadies who also fought with the band's roadies. Incidents included falling asleep on stage and insisting the band only perform acoustic bass songs, which led to the other members losing "faith" in him and quitting. "Then there was the time he fell asleep on stage, and then he got it into his head that all the band should do is acoustic bass songs, and that's when everybody around him in Faith No More had no more faith."

podcast.title: Comeback in Alternative Metal
podcast.body: Faith No More was mentioned as an older group that made a comeback in the 2010s, alongside Jane's Addiction and Biohazard, within the Alternative Metal/Alternative Hard Rock scene that was prominent in the 90s. This contributed to the renewed success of heavy bands from the past. "Plus we saw comebacks from older groups like Jane's Addiction, Biohazard and Faith No More to name a few."

podcast.body: Faith No More made significant contributions to the evolution of alt rock in the 1990s. "We cover the contributions of bands like the Beastie Boys and Faith No More."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Courtney Love's Brief Tenure
podcast.body: For a period, Courtney Love served as the band's front person, an interesting historical note given her later prominence. "A woman named Courtney Love was their front person for a time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Crossover Example
podcast.body: Faith No More was cited as one of the few existing examples of crossover between rock and hip-hop prior to the *Judgment Night* soundtrack in 1993. This context highlights how radical the concept of pairing rock and hip-hop acts was at the time. "Okay, yeah, there was the Beastie Boys, the version of Walk This Way with Aerosmith and Run DMC and some Faith No More."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Singer Changes
podcast.body: By 1983, the band, originally named Sharp Young Men, changed their name to Faith No More and brought in Chuck Mosley as singer. Mosley had replaced Courtney Love, who was part of the group for approximately 15 minutes. "He replaced a woman named Courtney Love, yes her, who was part of the group for about 15 minutes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Financial Motivation for Reunion
podcast.body: The decision to reunite was largely driven by financial incentives, as there is "no pension plan in rock," and reunion tours offer significant monetary returns. "Why did they try to decide to do this again? I'm going to guess that it was the universal reason. Money. Lots and lots of money."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hip Hop Experimentation
podcast.body: Faith No More was noted for their experimental approach, frequently incorporating hip hop sounds into their music, preceding the rise of genres like nu-metal. "Faith no more loved to experiment with hip hop sounds"

podcast.body: Faith No More is among the bands that have cited Fishbone as an important influence on their music. "Faith No More."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Members' Post-Breakup Projects
podcast.body: Following the breakup, members pursued various endeavors: other bands like Imperial Teen and Mr. Bungle were formed, some made guest appearances and received production credits, and record labels were established. Drummer Mike Bordin worked with Ozzy Osborne for a period, and guitarist Jim Martin transitioned to growing 1,300-pound pumpkins professionally. "Drummer Mike Bowden went off to work with Ozzy Osborne for a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Mike Bordin Introduces Dreadlocks to Metal
podcast.body: Mike Bordin, the former drummer for Faith No More, is widely acknowledged as the pioneer who introduced dreadlocks into the metal music genre in the late 1980s. "Mike Borden, the former German for Faith No More, is credited as being the guy who introduced dreads into metal in the late 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mike Patton Joins
podcast.body: After Chuck Mosley's departure, the remaining members reconvened and approached Mike Patton, who was the singer for Mr. Bungle and had met Faith No More in 1986. Patton joined as lead singer by January 1989, and promptly wrote all the lyrics for their next album in two weeks. "After the Mosley Fiasco, he was approached to become the lead singer, and by January 1989, he was in."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Pioneering Genre Fusion
podcast.body: By the mid-1980s, Faith No More was developing a distinctive sound combining "crunchy metallic guitars, heavy beats, and a rap style vocal delivery," a unique blend for its time that contributed to breaking down musical barriers. "By the mid-80s, they had a real thing going on, crunchy metallic guitars, heavy beats, and a rap style vocal delivery."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Genre Fusion
podcast.body: Faith No More was one of the earliest rock bands to successfully blend heavy guitars with rap-style vocals, an innovative approach that earned them retrospective recognition for their influence and importance. "They were one of the very first rock bands to realize that heavy guitars could be mixed with rap style vocals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Reunion for Touring
podcast.body: Faith No More was one of many bands from past decades that reunited in the 21st century, a trend largely motivated by financial incentives. With declining CD sales impacting artist revenues, returning to the touring circuit offered a lucrative way to appeal to nostalgic fan bases and fill large venues. "The list of reunions is long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Suburban Rap Introduction
podcast.body: Along with the Beastie Boys, Faith No More played a key role in making rap accessible to white suburban kids through their successful crossover songs like "Epic." "And just as we saw with the Beastie Boys, it found purchase with white kids in the suburbs."

xref.title: Influences on Mask Concept

They loved the anonymity that make up offered them. Another influence was the band Mr. Bungle, the group headed up by Mike Patton of Faith No More. They've been known to use masks and jumpsuits and pseudonyms too."

xref.title: Pre-Hole Career and Struggles
xref.body: Before finding her place with Hole, Courtney Love was involved in several bands, including Sugar Baby Doll and Babes in Toilet. She also had a very brief stint as the singer for Faith No More, lasting "about 15 minutes" before she was kicked out. To support herself and her early band efforts, she engaged in arts, acting, and stripping, using the money from stripping to purchase gear for her band. "She'd been in a bunch of bands with names like Sugar Baby Doll and Babes in Toilet."
